summary: Defines the format for writing literal IPv6 addresses inside URLs, for use in web browsers. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 3986.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2732 defines how to write a literal IPv6 address as the host in a URL: put the address inside square brackets. RFC 3986 later obsoleted RFC 2732.

questions: how to write an ipv6 address in a url
why are ipv6 addresses in brackets in urls
why are ipv6 addresses in square brackets
what changed in rfc 2396 for ipv6
subtitle: Square brackets mark a literal IPv6 address inside a URL.

tldr.problem: IPv6 address text and URL syntax both use colons and periods, so an IPv6 address needs a clear boundary when it appears as a URL host.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC encloses an IPv6 address in square brackets and updates RFC 2396's host syntax to allow that form.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2732 updates RFC 2396 and has been obsoleted by RFC 3986, which supersedes this syntax specification.

today: RFC 2732 has been obsoleted by RFC 3986. It updated RFC 2396.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Addresses Need Delimiters
sections.content:
The text form of a literal IPv6 address is not directly compatible with URLs because both use colon and period characters as delimiters. RFC 2732 sets out a form that allows an address to be copied into a URL with little editing.

The RFC says Web browsers SHOULD implement this format. Other applications and protocols that use URLs MAY use it.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 address text and URLs both use colons and periods. Square brackets make the address's boundaries clear when it is used as a URL host.

sections.title: Writing the Bracketed Address
sections.content:
Place [ before the literal IPv6 address and ] after it. For example, the RFC shows 1080::8:800:200C:417A as http://[1080::8:800:200C:417A]/foo.

A port number, when present in the URL, follows the closing bracket. The RFC also gives examples with embedded IPv4 address text inside the brackets.
sections.plainLanguage: Put square brackets around the complete IPv6 address in the URL host. If the URL has a port, write it after the closing bracket.

sections.title: Changes to the URI Host Syntax
sections.content:
RFC 2732 updates the generic URI syntax in RFC 2396. The host rule gains an IPv6 reference, defined as an IPv6 address inside square brackets, with the address form taken from RFC 2373.

The document replaces the IPv4 address definition with the RFC 2373 definition and moves square brackets into the reserved-character set, removing them from the unwise-character set.
sections.plainLanguage: The updated host rule accepts a bracketed IPv6 address. The RFC also adjusts the URI character rules so brackets are reserved for this syntax.

sections.title: Security and Current Status
sections.content:
The RFC says this way of representing IPv6 addresses introduces no known new security concerns. Its IANA Considerations section says there are no actions.

RFC 2732 updates RFC 2396 and is obsoleted by RFC 3986, according to the unit metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC reports no known new security concerns and requires no IANA action. RFC 3986 later replaced RFC 2732.

references.text: Hinden, R. and S. Deering, "IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture", RFC 2373, July 1998.
Fielding, R., Masinter, L. and T. Berners-Lee, "Uniform Resource Identifiers: Generic Syntax", RFC 2396, August 1998.
